beats.text: Neither needs a bug in Git. Each follows from what a merge is. A merge is computed from exactly three snapshots: your commit, their commit, and one common ancestor, called the merge base. Git's own FAQ says it plainly: "Git does not consider the history or the individual commits that have happened on those branches at all".

beats.text: The merge base. In one sentence: the merge base of two commits is their best common ancestor. That's the most recent commit that both histories contain, and the third input of every merge.
beats.tele: The merge base. In one sentence: the merge base of two commits is their best common ancestor. That's the most recent commit that both histories contain, and the third input of every merge.

beats.text: Precisely. A common ancestor of commits A and B is a commit reachable from both by following parents. The manual defines the rest: "One common ancestor is better than another common ancestor if the latter is an ancestor of the former. A common ancestor that does not have any better common ancestor is a best common ancestor, i.e. a merge base". Two branches have diverged when each contains commits that the other lacks.
beats.tele: Precisely. A common ancestor of commits A and B is a commit reachable from both by following parents. The manual defines the rest: "One common ancestor is better than another common ancestor if the latter is an ancestor of the former. A common ancestor that does not have any better common ancestor is a best common ancestor, i.e. a merge base". Two branches have diverged when each contains commits that the other lacks.

beats.text: Why is it an input? Without it, you can't tell what each side did. If a line is present on one side and absent on the other, was it added by the first or deleted by the second? Only the common starting point decides.
beats.tele: Why is it an input? Without it, you can't tell what each side did. If a line is present on one side and absent on the other, was it added by the first or deleted by the second? Only the common starting point decides.

Which commits are they? git log with --oneline, --left-right, and the same three dots.

beats.text: Inside .git. Nothing is stored. The merge base is computed from the parent lines of commit objects, every time a command needs it. No file says where a branch "came from".
beats.tele: Inside `.git`. Nothing is stored. The merge base is computed from the parent lines of commit objects, every time a command needs it. No file says where a branch "came from".

beats.text: Fast-forward. In one sentence: when your current commit is an ancestor of the commit you merge, there's nothing to combine. So Git moves your branch ref to that commit, and creates no new object.
beats.tele: Fast-forward. In one sentence: when your current commit is an ancestor of the commit you merge, there's nothing to combine. So Git moves your branch ref to that commit, and creates no new object.

beats.text: Precisely: the condition is git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD <other>. Put differently, the merge base is your own tip. Fast-forwarding is the default.
beats.tele: Precisely: the condition is `git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD <other>`. Put differently, the merge base is your own tip. Fast-forwarding is the default.

beats.text: "Already up to date." The opposite case has its own message. If the other commit is already an ancestor of HEAD, the merge prints "Already up to date." and moves nothing. Hold on to that message. It comes back at the end of the demo.

beats.text: So there are three cases, and ancestry decides between them. HEAD is an ancestor of the other: fast-forward. The other is an ancestor of HEAD: nothing to do. Neither: the branches have diverged, and you get a true merge, which the next video takes apart.
beats.tele: So there are three cases, and ancestry decides between them. HEAD is an ancestor of the other: fast-forward. The other is an ancestor of HEAD: nothing to do. Neither: the branches have diverged, and you get a true merge, which the next video takes apart.

beats.text: What a fast-forward changes in .git. The file refs/heads/main is rewritten with the new commit ID. ORIG_HEAD receives the old one. The reflogs of HEAD and of main each gain one line. The index and the working tree are updated as by a branch switch. The object database doesn't change.
beats.tele: What a fast-forward changes in `.git`. The file `refs/heads/main` is rewritten with the new commit ID. `ORIG_HEAD` receives the old one. The reflogs of HEAD and of `main` each gain one line. The index and the working tree are updated as by a branch switch. The object database doesn't change.

beats.text: One detail the textbook's authors found while testing: every git merge call rewrites ORIG_HEAD with the tip it started from, even a call that prints "Already up to date." or refuses. So as an undo pointer it's valid only until the next attempt. The reflog is the durable record.

beats.text: When a fast-forward is not what you want. The risk is the missing trace. If somebody fast-forwards an unfinished branch into main, the history looks as if the work-in-progress commits had been made on main directly, and no merge commit exists to revert. Nobody wants to discover that on a Friday evening. A later video shows how to forbid it.
beats.tele: When a fast-forward is not what you want. The risk is the missing trace. If somebody fast-forwards an unfinished branch into `main`, the history looks as if the work-in-progress commits had been made on `main` directly, and no merge commit exists to revert. Nobody wants to discover that on a Friday evening. A later video shows how to forbid it.

beats.text: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy for the merge base: two editors photocopy a manuscript on Monday, and mark up their copies separately. On Friday you can combine their work only if you still have the Monday copy. Without it, you can't tell a sentence that one editor added from a sentence that the other deleted. The merge base is the Monday copy.
beats.tele: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy for the merge base: two editors photocopy a manuscript on Monday, and mark up their copies separately. On Friday you can combine their work only if you still have the Monday copy. Without it, you can't tell a sentence that one editor added from a sentence that the other deleted. The merge base is the Monday copy.

beats.text: It breaks in two places. Git finds the Monday copy by walking parent links, not by date. And a tangled history can have two equally good Monday copies. That's the next video.
beats.tele: It breaks in two places. Git finds the Monday copy by walking parent links, not by date. And a tangled history can have two equally good Monday copies. That's the next video.

beats.text: And for the fast-forward: a bookmark in a manuscript that somebody else kept writing. You move the bookmark to the last page. It breaks on one point: nothing in the book records that the bookmark moved, or that the new pages were ever a separate branch. Only your local reflog knows.

beats.text: Three dots mean something different to git diff, and the difference matters for reviews. With three dots, git diff compares the merge base with the branch tip: what the branch did, and nothing that main did meanwhile. With two dots it compares the two tips, so the temperature change that main made appears as if the branch had undone it.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Expecting a merge commit after "Fast-forward". Root cause: the current tip was an ancestor of the other commit, so there was nothing to combine; one ref moved and no object was written.
beats.tele: Expecting a merge commit after "Fast-forward". Root cause: the current tip was an ancestor of the other commit, so there was nothing to combine; one ref moved and no object was written.

beats.text: Reading "Already up to date." as "the change is in my files". Root cause: the message is a statement about ancestry: the other commit is reachable from HEAD.
beats.tele: Reading "Already up to date." as "the change is in my files". Root cause: the message is a statement about ancestry: the other commit is reachable from HEAD.

beats.text: Using two dots in git diff to review a branch. Root cause: two dots compare the tips, so everything main did since the fork appears reversed; three dots compare from the merge base.
beats.tele: Using two dots in `git diff` to review a branch. Root cause: two dots compare the tips, so everything `main` did since the fork appears reversed; three dots compare from the merge base.

beats.text: Relying on ORIG_HEAD after a second merge attempt. Root cause: every git merge call rewrites ORIG_HEAD with the tip it started from; the reflog is the durable record.
beats.tele: Relying on `ORIG_HEAD` after a second merge attempt. Root cause: every `git merge` call rewrites `ORIG_HEAD` with the tip it started from; the reflog is the durable record.

beats.text: Fast-forwarding an unfinished branch into main. Root cause: the default allows it, and it leaves no merge commit to revert.
beats.tele: Fast-forwarding an unfinished branch into `main`. Root cause: the default allows it, and it leaves no merge commit to revert.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. The textbook draws two production consequences from the merge base.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. The textbook draws two production consequences from the merge base.

beats.text: First, the three-dot diff is what a pull request page shows. That's why a pull request doesn't list changes that landed on the base branch after you forked. It's GitHub's use of the same merge base.
beats.tele: First, the three-dot diff is what a pull request page shows. That's why a pull request doesn't list changes that landed on the base branch after you forked. It's GitHub's use of the same merge base.

beats.text: Second, the age of the merge base predicts merge pain. A branch on an evaluation team that forked three weeks ago is combined against a three-week-old snapshot, and everything both sides did since then is in play. So for a branch that must live long, merging main into it at intervals moves the merge base forward and keeps each merge small.
beats.tele: Second, the age of the merge base predicts merge pain. A branch on an evaluation team that forked three weeks ago is combined against a three-week-old snapshot, and everything both sides did since then is in play. So for a branch that must live long, merging `main` into it at intervals moves the merge base forward and keeps each merge small.

beats.text: And the fast-forward in daily life? It's what git pull does on a branch where you have no commits of your own.

beats.text: Let's land this. You should now be able to say: the merge base is the best common ancestor of two commits and the third input of every merge. It's computed from parent links, not stored. If my tip is an ancestor of the other commit, git merge fast-forwards: the branch ref moves, ORIG_HEAD and the reflogs record it, and no object is created.

beats.text: If the other commit is an ancestor of mine, Git says "Already up to date." and moves nothing. If neither is an ancestor of the other, the branches have diverged, and the merge creates a commit with two parents.
